_readme.covers: Units 22-26. Rated progressions for leading-tone seventh chords, mixture (borrowed chords in major), and applied dominants / applied leading-tone chords.
_readme.structure: Each rule has: id, quality, from, to, feedback.

matching.from: Root numerals for the previous chord. Empty list applies only to the first chord.
matching.to: Root numerals for the current chord.
matching.bare_root: A bare numeral like 'V' matches every inversion of V.
matching.figured: A numeral with a figure like 'V65' matches only that inversion.
matching.applied: Applied chords are written with a slash, e.g. 'V/V', 'V7/II', 'vii°7/V'.
matching.case: In minor keys the analyzer emits uppercase VII for the natural (modal) subtonic and lowercase vii for the raised (harmonic-minor) leading tone. Both forms are listed where a rule is intended to cover the seventh degree in either spelling.

how_to_add_a_rule: 1. Copy a rule block between { and }.
2. Give it a new unique id.
3. Set from and to as above.
4. Pick a quality: excellent, good, fair, discouraged, bad.
6. Save. No trailing comma after the last rule.

rules.feedback: Applied dominant of V resolving to V. The strongest way to intensify a cadential approach without leaving the home key. The applied leading tone rises by half step to the dominant's root.
Applied dominant of ii resolving to supertonic harmony. A characteristic opening gesture in the nineteenth-century repertoire.
Applied dominant of vi resolving to the submediant. Prepares a deceptive-sounding arrival or a brief tonicization of the relative minor.
Applied dominant of IV resolving to subdominant harmony. Common in major; in minor this tonicizes the major subdominant and mixes modes.
Applied dominant of iii resolving to the mediant. iii is the weakest diatonic goal, so the tonicization rarely stands on its own.

Applied dominant of the seventh degree. In minor keys the natural subtonic is a major triad (VII), so this is a modal cadence rather than a functional one; in major keys the target is the diminished leading-tone triad and the resolution is unusual.
Two applied dominants in succession. Characteristic of the extended tonicizations in Brahms and Wagner, but unusual in strict common-practice writing.
Diminished seventh chord on the applied leading tone resolving to V. The four voices each move by half step (or common tone) into the dominant, a striking chromatic effect.
Applied diminished seventh resolving to its target. Strong chromatic intensification, especially common at approach to a new key area.

Leading-tone seventh chord resolving to tonic. The leading tone rises to 1, the chordal seventh falls by step, and the remaining voices descend into the tonic triad. A defining chromatic gesture in minor and mixture.
Leading-tone seventh to dominant. The seventh of vii°7 (b6) should resolve down to 5, but V contains no 5-above-5 that can absorb the tendency cleanly — the direction feels stalled.
Half-diminished seventh resolving to tonic. Idiomatic in major, where the seventh (6) resolves down to 5 and the leading tone rises to 1. A characteristic bright chromatic colour.
Borrowed minor subdominant to dominant. b6 descends by step to 5, and the resulting chromatic tension drives into the cadence. A hallmark of mixture.
Borrowed minor subdominant to tonic — a plagal motion coloured by mixture. Common at the close of a phrase in major.
Borrowed flat-VI to dominant. b6 descends by step to 5 while the bass ascends, producing a strong chromatic approach to the cadence.
Flat-VI to minor subdominant. Both chords share the borrowed b6; the motion prolongs the plagal flavour of the parallel mode.
Borrowed flat-III to subdominant. Common in nineteenth-century repertoire but rare in strict common-practice writing.
Flat-VII to tonic. A modal borrowing that evokes popular and folk idioms. Rare in the classical style.
Flat-VII to dominant. Works as a chromatic approach to the cadence. In popular styles this pair is extremely common; in classical writing it is unusual.
Borrowed subdominant-family chord to a fully diminished seventh on the leading tone. Common chromatic preparation for a tonic arrival.
